mappings.note: How to find the pH of lemon juice. This is C 8.2-LO-1 almost word for word -- testing the pH of a household substance -- with LO-4 supplying the interpretation.
Bleaching powder losing chlorine on storage. A property of bleaching powder, LO-5.
Why sodium carbonate solution is basic -- salt of a weak acid and a strong base. The pH of a salt solution, LO-4, rather than LO-5's substance description.
Antacid relieving stomach pain. Everyday pH, LO-4.
What baking soda does to milk's pH. The pH shift is LO-4; baking soda as the agent is LO-5.
Pink phenolphthalein discharged by adding B: A is basic, B acidic. Indicator plus neutralisation, LO-3.
The compound made from gypsum that hardens with water -- plaster of Paris, its preparation equation and a use. LO-5 verbatim.
A soluble metal oxide leaving blue litmus unchanged is basic. Indicator evidence for basic nature, LO-3.
Tartaric acid's part in making a cake rise. Composition and use of baking powder, LO-5.
Plaster of Paris bandage setting on a fracture. A use of plaster of Paris, LO-5. (The stem has lost several words -- see defect list.)
The chlorine-smelling laundry whitener is bleaching powder, with its preparation equation. LO-5.
Tartaric acid in baking powder and gypsum in cement. Uses of LO-5's substances.
Washing soda effloresces in air. A property of washing soda, LO-5. (Duplicates 85000 -- see defect list.)
Chloride of lime versus calcium chloride, and why the former loses chlorine. Composition and properties of bleaching powder, LO-5.
The chemical property behind each use of baking soda. LO-5 names exactly this.

Copper sulphate crystals losing their water of crystallisation on heating. Blue vitriol is not one of LO-5's four named substances, so the competency on the nature and properties of substances is cited rather than stretching LO-5.
Blue litmus turning red on a knife used to cut fruit, so the fruit is acidic. Indicator evidence, LO-3.
Remedy for indigestion after spicy food. Everyday pH, LO-4.
Acids in ants, lemon, milk and tomato, plus two salts of the sodium family. Neither the natural sources of acids nor salt families has an outcome in this frame; competency cited.
Raising and lowering the pH of a neutral solution and reading a pH from a litmus change -- LO-4; part (c), a solution that frees CO2 from a carbonate, is the acid-carbonate reaction of LO-3.

Sticky salt, blue vitriol whitening, and a conc. H2SO4 bottle overflowing. All three turn on hygroscopic, deliquescent and water-of-crystallisation behaviour, which has no learning outcome in this frame.
The Solvay route to sodium carbonate, from raw materials to the final carbonate. Preparation of washing soda, LO-5.
Litmus on dry versus dissolved ammonia and precipitates from ammonium hydroxide -- indicator and base behaviour, LO-3; the dry-gas half turns on there being no ions without water, LO-4.
Parts (a)-(c) are conduction, hydronium concentration and the pH of concentrated versus dilute acid -- LO-4; part (d) observes acid on a hydrogencarbonate and on zinc, which is LO-3.
Dry versus moist litmus on HCl gas and the souring of milk are LO-4 (ions need water; pH change); the colour of blue litmus in sodium carbonate is an indicator reading, LO-3.

Brine electrolysis giving hydrogen and chlorine, and chlorine on dry slaked lime giving bleaching powder -- LO-5. The equation asked for is electrolysis, not a neutralisation, so C 1.3 rather than C 1.3-LO-3.
Strong versus weak acids is LO-4; identifying NaOH and writing its balanced neutralisation with dilute HCl is C 1.3-LO-3.
Name, formula, sources and uses of common salt. Common salt is not one of LO-5's four substances -- it is their raw material -- so the C 1.2 competency is cited rather than forcing LO-5.
The chlor-alkali process, its equation, products and uses. The products are LO-5's feedstocks; the equation is electrolysis, so the C 1.3 competency rather than its neutralisation LO.
Colour of neutral litmus solution. Indicator behaviour, LO-3.
Which indicator is olfactory. Indicators, LO-3.
Which method gives an accurate pH. Choosing the right instrument is the planning half of C 8.2-LO-1; LO-4 supplies what pH means.
Correct statement about the universal indicator. Reading the pH scale, LO-4.
Which properties dilute HCl shows -- litmus, zinc, sodium carbonate. Exactly LO-3's list of acid behaviours.
Metallic oxides are basic, non-metallic oxides acidic. Classification by acid-base character, LO-3.
Deep red on pH paper means strongly acidic. Reading a pH-paper colour, LO-4.
Drinking water at pH 6 must have had something acidic added. Relating pH to nature, LO-4.
Dry solid sodium bicarbonate on pH paper leaves it unchanged -- no water, no ions (LO-4). It is also a point of pH-testing technique, C 8.2-LO-1.
Which sample turns red litmus blue. Indicator test for a base, LO-3.
Which sample's pH cannot be read directly from pH paper. A limitation of the measuring technique, C 8.2-LO-1, with LO-4 behind it.
Which natural source holds oxalic acid. Sources of acids have no outcome in this frame; competency cited, as with 84979 and 85013.
The acid in an ant sting. Taught under pH in everyday life, LO-4, consistent with the other sting items.
What to take for acidity. Everyday pH, LO-4.
Products of potassium sulphate with barium iodide -- a salt-salt double displacement. Not a neutralisation nor an acid on metal or carbonate, so C 1.3-LO-3 does not apply and the competency is cited.
Which salt is basic. The pH of a salt solution, LO-4.
Which salt has the lowest pH. The pH of a salt solution, LO-4.
What is needed to identify the gas from zinc and dilute HCl (a burning splinter). The acid-metal reaction and its test, LO-3.
Zinc giving hydrogen with both acid and base means it is amphoteric. The acid-metal and base-metal behaviour of LO-3.
Which of four solutions turns the universal indicator red. Reading the pH scale, LO-4.
pH of water after dissolving sodium bicarbonate rises above 7. Relating a substance to pH, LO-4.
What happens when acid and base solutions are mixed -- neutralisation giving salt and water. LO-3's 'with each other'.
Methyl orange is red in acid. Indicator colours, LO-3.
Phenolphthalein is pink in base. Indicator colours, LO-3.
Egg shells fizzing to give a gas that turns lime water milky identifies an acid. Acid on a carbonate, LO-3. (Duplicates 84928 -- see defect list.)
Why universal indicator beats litmus -- it gives a pH value, not just acid or base. The pH scale, LO-4.
Water-soluble bases are alkalis. Defining bases, LO-3.
Which pair gives table salt -- hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide. Neutralisation, LO-3.
Universal indicator colour at pH 1. Reading the pH scale, LO-4.
Which medicine treats indigestion. Everyday pH, LO-4. (Duplicates 84930 -- see defect list.)
Gas from magnesium with hydrochloric acid. The acid-metal reaction of LO-3.
